title: The colour of the light — Image Wiki
text:
The colour of the light
  What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.

  
    Termilluminant colour / local colour
    Also calledcolour temperature, colour cast, white balance, colour constancy
    Not the same aslocal colour vs the colour you see, warm/cool as a rule vs as a case, exposure
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensTwo light sources, two coloursThe rest of the environment is a light source tooWhat white balance actually doesCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Wear a white shirt to breakfast under a kitchen bulb, walk outside at noon, stand under a streetlight at midnight. You call it white all three times. Photograph it with the camera locked on daylight and you get three files: one orange, one neutral, one sickly yellow-green.
The light was completely different every time and your eye hid that from you. Cameras and renderers do not hide it.
Why it happens
What reaches your eye from a surface is a product of two things: the mix of wavelengths in the light, and the percentage of each wavelength the surface reflects. That second one is local colour — the shirt's own whiteness, the apple's own redness, the part that stays put when you carry the apple into another room. You never see local colour directly. You only ever see the product.

surfacelightyou see×=white paperchroma 2×=scarletchroma 75×=cyan-bluechroma 50neutral daylight, about 6500 KUnder neutral lightevery surface shows its own coloursurfacelightyou see×=white paperchroma 56×=scarletchroma 84×=cyan-bluechroma 15a tungsten bulb, about 2700 KUnder warm lightthe same three surfaces, one light changed

The multiplication, worked out channel by channel in linear light: the same three surfaces under a neutral 6500 K illuminant and under a 2700 K bulb.
The neutral is the giveaway — the paper has nothing of its own to contribute, so its chroma goes from 2 to 56 and it simply becomes the colour of the bulb. The scarlet barely moves; the light is already near its hue. The blue collapses: it sits near the light's opposite, so most of what it would have reflected is not in the light at all. Chroma falls from 50 to 15 and it lands as a dark grey-green, not a dark blue. That last row is the one people get wrong when they invent a colour cast by hand.


Your visual system then does the division. It works out from everything in view what the light is probably doing, and discounts it. That is colour constancy, good enough that most people never notice indoor light is orange. Strobist's Lighting 103 opens on the line Sara Lando brought back from assisting Gregory Heisler: white light is a lie.
One consequence worth naming separately: the total range of colour shrinks under a tinted light. If you see a wide spread of hues anyway, the light was not that tinted. This is also most of what a "limited palette" really is — see How to choose colours.


Direct sun: Rouen Cathedral, West Façade, Sunlight
Diffuse sky: Rouen Cathedral, West Façade


Claude Monet, two canvases from the Rouen Cathedral series, both 1894, both public domain. Left: National Gallery of Art, Washington. Same building, same viewpoint, same grey limestone — Monet painted the series to record the light changing.
Left, in direct sun, the stone comes out cream and pale gold, while the recesses of the three portals — cut off from the sun, lit only by sky — go blue-violet.
Right, with the sun off the façade, that same stone reads lavender-blue almost everywhere and the sky becomes the warm note, a pale cream. What direct light remains is the salmon-pink down the ribs of the left tower. Warm and cool have swapped sides without anything in the scene moving.


Two light sources, two colours
Outdoors on a clear day there are two lights. The sun is a small warm source from one direction; the sky is an enormous blue source from everywhere. A surface facing the sun gets sun plus sky. A surface in shadow is cut off from the sun and lit almost entirely by sky — which is why the shadow edge is crisp and its interior smooth: the sources differ in apparent size as much as in colour (Hard and soft light).
So a shadow is not the lit side minus some light. It is the lit side under a different illuminant, and the colour temperatures back it up: sun overhead runs 5000–6500 K, open shade under a clear sky 9000–10000 K. See The anatomy of a shadow.



Claude Monet, The Magpie, 1868–69. Musée d'Orsay, Paris. Public domain.
Snow is the cleanest test surface there is, because its local colour is near-white: any colour you can see in it came from the light. Follow the shadow the gate casts down and to the right across the foreground, and the shadowed face of the snow-drifted wall at the far left. Both are unmistakably blue-lilac while the snow beside them is a warm cream — there is no neutral grey in the snow anywhere.
Not the same light dimmed. The lit snow sees the low sun plus the sky; the shadowed snow sees only the sky, and reports its colour faithfully.



Warm light, cool shadows is a common case, not a rule
It inverts constantly. Under an overcast sky the whole dome is the source, so there is barely a shadow and no warm/cool split at all. A face lit by a monitor in a dark room has a cool key, and whatever warm lamp is behind it fills the shadow. Indoors at dusk, a 2700 K table lamp beside the sitter and 6500 K daylight through the window puts the warm side wherever you moved the lamp. Check the picture; do not recite the maxim.




Georges de La Tour, The Penitent Magdalene with a Night Light, c. 1640–45. Musée du Louvre. Public domain (Web Gallery of Art reproduction).
The single-source case, with no cool fill at all. Read the light off the neutral: her chemise is white linen. Where it faces the lamp, high on her chest, it is cream; along her far sleeve, amber-gold; beyond that, brown and then black. Not one blue note in the whole garment. With no second light the dark side of every form falls away to nothing, which is why a room lit by one flame reads as a far smaller world than a sunlit street.


The rest of the environment is a light source too
At midday in a city the light has bounced off the buildings before it reaches anyone — Strobist's Havana walk describes ochre walls acting as giant amber fill cards, so even "white" noon sun arrives warm at street level. With the sun low, its light crosses far more atmosphere, which scatters out the blue and leaves gold, while the shade in the same frame is lit by cool open sky. The two sides of the street pull further apart as the day goes on.
Gurney has the counter-case: the shadow side of an ochre building in Toledo, drenched in light reflected off an orange building opposite, comes out more saturated than the same wall in full sun. The painters' maxim "colour obtains in the light" usually holds, and bounce breaks it.

Sources disagree on why
Gurney attributes the drop in shadow chroma to colour receptors responding less at low light levels; the vision scientist he asked, Jack Werner, replied that the effect is more complicated and partly comes from lateral interactions between the lit and shadowed patches. There is also a purely geometric account with no physiology in it: as a surface turns out of the light, value and chroma fall together along a shading series (Hue, value and chroma). Probably all three contribute.

What white balance actually does
The camera has no brain to do the division, so it is told which colour of light counts as white and divides that back out. Set it to tungsten and the file assumes 3200 K; shoot that under neutral light and everything comes out blue.
Auto white balance guesses by pushing the frame's average toward neutral, which fails exactly when the guess is wrong: point it at a wall of red autumn leaves and it "corrects" a scene that was never wrong. Under mixed lighting there may be no correct answer — balance a night scene off the moon and the sodium-lit building goes deep orange, balance off the stone and the sky goes an unreal blue. Both files are defensible.
It is also a creative control. Strobist's standard trick is to shift the camera's white balance one way to recolour the whole ambient environment, then gel the flash the complementary way, over-gelling slightly so the subject reads warm against a blue world.
Common mistakes

"The shadow is the local colour plus black." It is the local colour under a second, usually differently coloured light. Grey versions of the lit side are the fastest way to make an image look flat and fake.
"An orange cast means the white balance is wrong." Sunset is orange, candlelight sits around 1000–2000 K. Correcting that away deletes the information about when and where you are.
"Auto white balance is the objective answer." It is an average-based guess that one dominant colour will defeat.
"You can read the light's colour off a coloured object." Read it off the neutrals — a white shirt, a grey road, concrete, the whites of eyes.


How to read the light in five seconds

Find something you know is neutral. What colour is it in this image? That is your light.
Find a shadow. Compare its hue to the lit side of the same object — different hue, or only darker?
Count sources. Do all the shadows in the frame agree about direction and colour?
Look at the specular highlights: they carry the light's own colour, not the object's.
If lit and shadow differ only in darkness, and every neutral in frame is perfectly grey, suspect a render with one white light — or a composite. See Naming what is wrong.

              A colour is not one thing. It is three independent dials — which colour it is, how light it is, and how far it sits from grey — and most arguments about colour are two people turning different dials.
